other_side: Where NLW sees a cavalcade of models as raw material for a nimble multi-model stack, Zitron's piece of the previous day sees the same launches as the mechanism of a bubble: AI start-ups that resell tokens at a loss are, he says, 'a venture-backed marketing platform for the latest models', so each launch spikes lab revenue without any customer paying out of cashflow. He points to the very events in this edition, Cursor's cut-off by OpenAI after the SpaceX purchase and Cognition's doubling in valuation, as evidence that a few hundred subsidised customers carry the labs, which in turn carry the hyperscalers and Nvidia, with at least two hundred billion dollars of compute bills falling due in 2027. Choosing between models, in his telling, is a luxury paid for by someone else's losses.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether model abundance is a healthy market or a subsidised one. Both accept as fact that six frontier releases in nine days is unprecedented, that cost per task now matters as much as capability, and that the biggest buyers of tokens are AI companies such as Cursor and Cognition rather than ordinary enterprises. The empirical question that will resolve is whether cheap, fast models like Gemini 3.8 Flash and MuSpark expand demand from non-AI businesses or merely shift existing start-up spend between labs; the observable is Ramp's customer-concentration figure and the labs' disclosed enterprise revenue mix over the next two quarters. The worldview residue is whether a benchmark-gamed cheap model is a bargain or a warning sign. NLW is vindicated if non-tech firms visibly build multi-model stacks and pay for them; Zitron if 2027's compute commitments trigger visible retrenchment. Both are polemicists with incentives, one bullish and anti-doom, the other bubble-certain and anti-hype, and both flag the same trust problem: who trains on your work. Watch the Cursor revenue gap at OpenAI.
